outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 answers, narrows, or moves a bound on whether a positive integer can be written as a sum of two positive fifth powers in more than one way; the last known computational bound (Ekl, 1998, sums checked up to roughly 4.01×10^30) and Guy's 1994/2004 statement of the open problem remain the most current record.
summary: The problem (Wikipedia's Taxicab(5,2,n), i.e. does any positive integer equal a sum of two positive fifth powers in more than one way) remains unresolved and no genuine progress toward it was found since 26 January 2024. The triage flagged Benfield, Lippard & Roy, 'End behavior of Ramanujan's taxicab numbers' (arXiv:2404.08190, published The Ramanujan Journal 2024/2025) as a possible lead. Reading the abstract and attempting the full text: that paper's framework fixes k (the exponent) and studies what happens as j (the number of summands) grows, asking for which m (number of representations) a smallest Taxicab(k,j,m) exists; it is not about fixed j=2 and varying n (our question's axis), and no passage found addresses k=5, j=2 specifically. Wikipedia's own 'Generalized taxicab number' article still states, unchanged, that no number is known to be a sum of two fifth powers in more than one way and it is not known whether one exists, citing Guy's 2004 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' — the same pre-window source. MathWorld's page on the 5th-power Diophantine equation and ProofWiki likewise still cite only Guy (1994/1997) for the 1.02×10^26 (later corrected/extended in the literature to Ekl's 1998 bound of roughly 4.01×10^30) exhaustive-search bound, both predating the window; no updated search bound was found. I also checked two adjacent December 2025 preprints by Valery Asiryan that surfaced via search for 'equal sums of like powers': 'The Linear Slicing Method for Equal Sums of Like Powers' (arXiv:2512.00551) and its companion 'Genus-One Fibrations and the Jacobian of Linear Slices in the Quintic Equal-Sum Problem' (arXiv:2512.11072). The second paper studies a^5+b^5=c^5+d^5 restricted to a single linear slice (c+d)-(a+b)=30 (the first admissible slice under a divisibility condition), and explicitly disclaims addressing 'the global open problem of non-trivial solutions ... without linear constraints'; moreover, even on that one restricted slice, the paper only bounds the Mordell-Weil rank of an associated elliptic surface at 1 and states this 'by itself ... does not decide the existence (or nonexistence) of integral solutions.' This is technical machinery-building on a narrow constrained sub-case that itself remains undecided — it does not remove any territory from the stated existence question, so it does not qualify as a case settled under §3.1. A third candidate, 'Ramanujan, the taxicab problem for polynomials, and the abc-conjecture' (arXiv:2604.25017), turned out on inspection to be about polynomial-ring identities p^n+q^n=r^n+s^n over ℤ[x]/ℂ[x], a formally different (variant) problem over different objects, not the integer question — excluded as a related problem rather than a case. No AI system was found credited in any of these papers; the Asiryan papers describe verification via the Magma computer algebra system, which is not an AI system under §6.2. Overall: status open, no_change_found true, confidence high that the specific existence question is untouched, though the broader 'equal sums of like powers' research area saw incremental structural work in 2024-2025 that does not bear on this bullet.
competing_reading: One could argue the Asiryan quintic-slice paper (arXiv:2512.11072) constitutes 'progress' in the loose sense that it is new mathematics narrowing possible solutions on one specific linear slice (h=30) of the same equation family. But the paper itself says this does not decide existence even on that slice, and a single slice out of infinitely many admissible h-values is a vanishingly small and non-exhaustive restriction; under the case-vs-variant test in §3.1 ('does this change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry?') the honest answer is no, so I classified as open rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an exhibited pair of positive integers with a^5+b^5 = c^5+d^5 and {a,b}≠{c,d} (would resolve as refuted/resolved), (b) a proof of nonexistence for all n>1 (resolved/confirmed), or (c) an extension of the exhaustive computational search bound beyond Ekl's ~4.01×10^30 published after 26 January 2024, which would count as `progress` under the record-is-the-question exception in §3.1 since Taxicab(5,2,n) as literally posed on Wikipedia's list is an existence/infinitude-style question but the underlying search-bound record is itself sometimes treated as the tracked quantity in this literature; I found no such updated bound.
